title: What're some older films that genuinely captivated you and held your attention?

commenti.body: [removed]
[removed]

Obvious ones that won’t surprise anyone are *Casablanca, It Happened One Night,* and *It’s a Wonderful Life.* I watched *On the Waterfront* three times this year. *Treasure of the Sierra Madre.* Lots more, but these immediately came to mind.

Metropolis (1927 Fritz Lang). It really is a classic that inspired many. Compelling and captivating with a magnificent score, based upon the three films you liked, you will likely not be able to look away.

Ben-Hur (1959 William Wyler). This film has it all. Compelling characters, well acted, epic story, bombastic score, cutting edge cinematography that holds up today.

2001 (1968 Stanley Kubrick). This is the classic slow burn. Some find it boring, but I find it compelling and very re-watchable. If you can see it in 70mm Cinerama it is a revelation. A masterclass in film making.

For years I had heard that Night of the Hunter from 1955 was one of the all time great noir crime thrillers. Finally threw it on one night a couple of years ago and it was...fine? A little dated but I was enjoying it , recognized a couple of things that had been parodied on The Simpsons etc. But I didn't at all see what was so hyped about it.

And then. And then! Right at the mid point there's a shot ( I won't spoil but you know it when you see it) that made me gasp and sit forward in excitement. It's truly one of the great shots in the history of cinema. And everything from there onwards is like a fever dream long chase sequence.

* Drama: "Treasure of the Sierra Madre" & "Casablanca"
* Western: "The Searchers" and "Once Upon a Time in the West"
* Noire: "Double Indemnity" and "The Killing" (1956)
* Comedy: "Bringing Up Baby" and "Some Like it Hot"
* War: "The Bridge on the River Kwai" and "Paths of Glory"
* SciFi: "The Day the Earth Stood Still" (1951) and "2001, A Space Odyssey"

Here are some excellent older films that are accessible:

Raoul Walsh was a versatile studio director, but truly excelled at action pictures. Objective, Burma! stars Errol Flynn as a the leader of a group of Army paratroopers who have to escape through hellish jungle after faulty intel strands them see behind enemy lines.

If you haven’t seen Alfred Hitchcock’s films, watch Rear Window and Psycho. For the latter, go in with as little knowledge as possible. And make sure you see his version (1960) not the remake.
Anthony Mann directed many fantastic pictures starring James Stewart, but the Naked Spur is probably the best. Stewart plays a bounty hunter on the trail of criminals in remote country. It’s a rare western that’s entirely set in the wildness. It uses the landscape spectacularly and Stewart delivers a truly incredible performance.

Rotten Tomatoes is a good place to find good old movies by a particular director or actor. I knew James Cagney was great in Public Enemy, White Heat and Angels With Dirty Faces, but I'd never have found out about Strawberry Blonde or Footlight Parade without searching for his best movies. You have two great early Kubrick movies listed. Folks who like those will probably also like The Killers and Brute Force (both star Burt Lancaster who is also great in Vera Cruz).

It was probably the fact that it was Saturady 1am (after a friday), and I REALLY wanted to see something. I didn't know shit about this movie (it was in HBOMax), but the name was interesting, it has Marlon Brando in it (I still didn't knew who Vivien Leigh was), and seemed to have that old-comfy-hollywood charm.

I also though it was a romantic comedy. Hell no, as the film progressed, it got worse and worse. Those were some intense hours in the night. I didn't know it was a theater play, so that intensity in the dialogue caught me off guard. And the whole atmostphere—the theatrical/method acting, the black and white cinematography with beautiful use of shadows, the fact that it looks like a set has some kind of charm, the jazzy soundtrack—sinks you into a unique experience.

The Big Sleep - moves fast like modern pictures and clicks like jazz in syncopated storytelling to create magnificent mood over clockwork logic. It is Hollywood in exelcis.

The Sweet Smell of Success - its cynicism and spin on the power of influence and promotion to sway opinion and curry favour ring as true today as ever. Match me, Sidney.

Sunset Boulevard - a peep behind the gates of the once great and not so good in the company of the almost was but never to be, illustrates the fleeting fickle nature of fame and fortune.

Lift to the Scaffold - Miles improvises over beautiful people making bad decisions as they attempt to escape to a life less ordinary.

Throne of Blood - Shakespearian samurai and their wicked wives conspire towards their own unavoidable destruction as forests encroach on impending doom.

Gentlemen Prefer Blondes - Monroe makes whoopee in a world where men maybe marks and women marksmen but true love slips into pole position for both.

Brief Encounter - what might have been but never was, captured in shades of silver to be replayed on an endless maudlin memory loop forever.

La Regle du Jeu - comedies of manners make a mockery of class in a very big house in the country.

King Kong - the original scream queen and most lovable monster escape an undiscovered island only to encounter inevitable tragedy at the apex of a metaphorical icon in a time when the world still contained mysteries.

Old movies, yeah! Here are some of my favorites. You *must* check them out! 

* The Third Man (1949) - I watch this one probably once a year. Maybe a perfect film. Suspenseful & witty script, great acting from Joseph Cotten & Orson Welles, twists & turns, and a classic chase scene through the Vienna sewers with amazing night-time cinematography. And the final shot! Oh my. 
* Yojimbo (1961) - I was going to say Seven Samurai but you already got that one, so this would be my next Kurosawa choice. Toshiro Mifune is spectacular (and hilarious) as a cynical but noble bad-ass who plays two gangs against each other. I fell in love with this film right off the bat, when Toshiro strolls into town and a dog crosses his path with a severed hand in its mouth. So cool. 
* Brief Encounter (1945)  - Some of the dialogue may seem a bit overwrought to modern ears, but this is a heartbreaking & subtle drama about two strangers who have a brief affair that's destined to never go anywhere. I was quite surprised when i first saw it how non-judgmental it is, given the year it was filmed. Trevor Howard and Celia Johnson are perfect together. 
* Night And The City (1950) - Oh man, this one is so good! Richard Widmark puts in a legendary performance as a sleazy hustler in London who gets in over his head. My favorite noir by a mile. Schemes, double-crosses, bad decisions, and more insanely gorgeous night-time cinematography as our hero (not really) runs for his life. 
* Arsenic And Old Lace (1944) - One of my top 5 all-time favorite comedies. Cary Grant is very funny as a newlywed who discovers that his kindly aunts may not be as sweet as they seem, and his creepy brother returns home to hide from the law. The insanity ratchets up at a perfect pace. I watch this every Halloween. 
* Night Of The Hunter (1955) - Very weird, very creepy and yet also dreamlike thriller with Robert Mitchum as a madman preacher pursuing two kids with ill intent.  The hymn "Leaning On The Everlasting Arms" will forever send chills down my spine, thanks to this brilliant film.

Lawrence of Arabia was my first great cinematic disappointment. All these years, you hear it’s great, the best thing ever. Then it’s just a guy in the desert, they’re talking about war (?), then (?). So boring. Great music and filming. But I could just go to the symphony and museum. The story is so dull. He goes there (?), there’s unrest. Then the rest is the music and filming. Boring. It’s a Nomadland situation where the whole thing you keep wondering where the plot is going, who’s about to do what. But nobody really does anything. A film about nothing. Gorgeous hubris. Except not really because who is doing what? Why? And who cares. A Streetcar Named Desire, a teacher sex pest moves to the city, tries to make it work, goes to the psych ward. Boom. Now, Voyager, a woman gets a makeover after detox, likes a guy, then decides to stay single and like his kid. Lawrence of Arabia incinerates your soul the whole time because it’s so dull.

A few I can think of that hopefully not many others are saying:

I am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang (1932) -- a really brilliant crime film with a scathing message of the state of America at the time, sneaking in right before the code censored movies deemed anti-American or anti-capitalist. almost a century later and it still has one of the most powerful endings I've ever seen -- probably my choice for most powerful final line of dialogue. point blank.

Out of the Past (1947) -- tbh I don't remember much about this other than that I liked it. if ur into noirs there's a good chance you'll dig it.

Un Chant d'Amour (1950) -- the only film by prolific queer writer Jean Genet and it's one of the most magnetic and inspired pieces of filmmaking I've ever seen. definitely watch the version with the moroccan jazz song (the original release was entirely silent, but Genet later approved the jazz song and to me it makes it so much more energetic). you don't have to be queer to like it, but it probably helps since you'd be watching a bunch of naked prisoners dancing to one another as a way to express freedom despite the bars

**The Producers** (1967) *Dir Mel Brooks.* A very funny film about the creative exploitation of tax loopholes. Zero Mostel and Gene Wilder work really well together.  
**Tengoku to jigoku** / **High and Low** (1963)  *Dir Akira Kurosawa*. An absolutely  captivating and surprisingly humane thriller from the master of cinema himself. I feel like Scorsese and Fincher must've seen this masterpiece.  
**L'année dernière à Marienbad** / **Last Year at Marienbad** (1961). *Dir Alain Resnais.* A hypnotic movie experience you want to relive again and again in the hopes of understanding it a little bit better. I bet Kaurismäki and Lynch love this movie.

**Rear Window** (1954) *Dir Alfred Hitchcock*. My favourite from Hitchock. It's such a blast of excitiment and thrills from first frame to the last. And it still looks as gorgeous as it feels. This is a must see!
